title: The Tools and the Harness
segs: Chapter 45. The Tools and the Harness.

Tanvi Kulkarni joined Imran Qureshi's team on a Monday in March. By Wednesday she had a question she was embarrassed to ask. At the whiteboard, in the voice of someone confessing, she said there were about seventeen tools in the team channel, and everybody mentioned them as if she already knew them. Which ones did she need to learn?
Imran capped his pen and put it down. For the first time Anaya had seen, he looked pleased by a question. "None of them," he said. "Not yet. Learn the slots."

This chapter follows Tanvi's first month. It starts with a way of thinking about tools and ends with a weekly report that went to customers. Between the two, it explains the structure around a model that turns it into a product.
The case: seventeen tools in a channel.
The names that worried Tanvi would change within a year. What would not change was the set of jobs those names were hired to do. So Imran's answer was to teach the jobs first.
Slots, not brands.

Imran drew a column of boxes. In each he wrote a verb phrase instead of the name of a product. Tanvi copied them into a notebook and saw that most of the names she had been worried about had vanished. An AI product, he said, needs about eleven things done for it, from the first idea to the last complaint.

Table 45.1: Eleven jobs, and what each must do. Reason and draft. What it must do: Work over the text you give it. Answer from sources. What it must do: Answer only from sources you upload, with citations you can check. Make a screen. What it must do: Turn a description into a working screen quickly enough for a user to try. Edit code. What it must do: Read your code, edit files and run commands while a person watches. Connect a process. What it must do: Join a trigger, a call, a check and an approval into a process that runs the same way every time. Test a request. What it must do: Send an exact request and save the answer as a repeatable test. Keep versions. What it must do: Keep every version of the code and review each change. Deploy. What it must do: Deploy on every push and roll back in minutes. Store data. What it must do: A database with sign-in, tables and rules about who may see which row. Record events. What it must do: Record events and draw funnels. Follow a request. What it must do: Follow one request from end to end, with what it cost and how long it took.

Thinking of tools as slots like this gives you a toolchain: the set of tools that builds and runs the product. Each slot has a job. For each job the team had picked one tool that quarter, because it did the job well enough and the team knew it. Next year the name in the slot might differ. The slot would still be there.

Tanvi asked why they didn't keep the choice open and use them all. Imran said she would then learn the interfaces and not the jobs. Most projects use five or six of the eleven. The mistake is to treat each box as a subject to master. A box is a place to put a tool. Ask what the job must do and what must never go wrong when it does it. Then choose the tool, and learn the job.
Anaya, listening from her desk, recognised the lesson she had been given in her first week about requirements: describe the job before you name the tool.
Two audits.
Imran gave Tanvi two habits to carry from job to job. The first came from a mistake of Anaya's.

The month before, Anaya had uploaded Mr. Menon's security questionnaire, forty pages long, to a research assistant that answers only from the documents it is given. It wrote a tidy summary and attached a source to every sentence. She had been rather proud of it. Imran asked her to carry out a claim audit. You pick ten claims from the summary, check each one against the page it cites, and mark it supported, partly supported or unsupported.

It took forty minutes. Seven claims were supported. Two were partly supported, because the page said something similar but narrower. One was unsupported: the summary said the lender required a particular certificate, and nothing in the document said so.
Key idea: One in ten is the limit.
If more than one or two claims in ten are unsupported, stop trusting that process for decisions, whichever tool produced it. If fewer, you may use it, and the team has learned what to check by hand.
The second habit was the secrets-and-data audit. For every tool in the stack, write down what it stores and where its keys live. The list that afternoon was longer than Anaya liked.

Table 45.2: The secrets-and-data audit. Code host. What it holds: Code and no secrets, which Imran proved by searching the history. Hosting company. What it holds: The model key and the database key as settings, and request logs. Database. What it holds: Accounts and results, with a rule on each table. Analytics tool. What it holds: Events and account numbers and no message text, which Karan had already confirmed. Model provider. What it holds: The text of every message sent for checking, so its retention policy mattered, and Anaya had read it twice.

Then Tanvi, who had been quiet, opened the demonstration page in her browser, pressed a key and went very still. In the script on the page she saw a long string that looked like a key. It was the key.

The tool that had turned a description into a screen in January had put the model provider's secret into code that is sent to every visitor. Anyone with a browser could read it. It had also created a database with no rule on who could read what. Imran changed the key within the hour, moved the call behind the server and wrote both findings in the log. Prototypes tend to do this, he said, so check before you share a link.
What is around the model.

On Thursday Imran gave Tanvi her first real task. He began by taking away a phrase she was about to use: "the AI does it". The model takes in text and gives out text, he said, and that is all it does. Everything else that makes a product work is built around it.
That surrounding structure is the harness. It has seven parts, and a person debugging a product should be able to find each one. The table names them, with the Monday report as the example.

Table 45.3: The seven parts of a harness, with the Monday report as the example. Context. What it does: Builds what the model sees on each call. In the Monday report: The week's counts, last week's counts, the instructions. Tools. What it does: Lets the model read or act. In the Monday report: Fetch the week's numbers; look up a customer's plan. State. What it does: Remembers across steps and across weeks. In the Monday report: Last week's figures; which customers have been done. Orchestration. What it does: Decides what runs next. In the Monday report: Gather, then draft, then check, then send. Policy. What it does: Rules the model cannot override. In the Monday report: Nothing is sent without approval; no message text in logs. Evals. What it does: Checks quality before and after a change. In the Monday report: Twenty past weeks, with reports a person wrote. Observability. What it does: Records what happened. In the Monday report: A trace per run, with tokens, cost and time.
Two products can use the same model and behave nothing alike, Imran said, because of this table. Nearly every quality problem you chase is in the table, not in the model.

The task itself was the Monday email Anaya had described in the winter, the one line telling a compliance buyer how many details the guard had hidden. It was to become a proper weekly report, with a count, a trend and a short list of unsure cases.
How coding assistants are built.

To do the work, Tanvi was to use a coding assistant. This is a program that reads a repository, edits files and runs commands while a person watches. Imran said it was worth understanding how these are made. They are the most widely used agents, and their design holds patterns that any product can borrow.

At the centre is a simple loop. The model chooses a tool. The harness runs it. The result goes back to the model, and the cycle repeats until the work is done. The tools are few and general: read a file, change a file, search, run a command. A handful of flexible tools turns out to beat dozens of narrow ones.

The rules of the project live in a plain file kept with the code, which the assistant reads at the start of every run. This is the project memory. Tanvi's first act was to open it and add a line: never write message text to a log.
There are also permission modes. Reading is allowed freely, while changing a file or running a command can require someone to say yes.

Imran called the most important part the verifier. A verifier is a check, such as a test or a type check, that tells the assistant whether its change worked, without a person reading every line. An assistant with a reliable way to check its own work can be given much larger jobs. One without it needs a human at every step, and then no speed has been gained.

When a job is large, the work can be divided. A sub-agent takes one part, works in its own separate context and returns only the result. That keeps the main conversation small and clear. None of this, Imran said, is about intelligence. It is about the loop, the memory and the check, and all of it could be used in the report.
Where the fences go.

The next lesson came from a story in the news that week. An assistant ran on someone's own computer, with the run of their files, their messages and their shell. It could do almost anything, which made it useful. It could also do almost anything, which made it dangerous. Tanvi drew four questions on the whiteboard as Imran gave them, and the table shows each question with the control that answers it.

Table 45.4: Four questions about a tool's reach. Which tools may it call? The control: An allowlist: a list of the only things the system may do, with anything not on it refused. With what scope? The control: Read-only where possible; one folder, one channel, one customer. Which calls need a person's approval? The control: Anything that sends, deletes, pays or cannot be undone. What can reach it? The control: Any text it reads, such as tickets, email or a web page, may contain orders written by an attacker.

Anaya recognised the last question as the trifecta of Chapter 24: private data, text from outsiders and a way to send. For every combination of tools, she said, at least one of the three must be removed.

Imran added that the team should start narrow and widen only on evidence chosen in advance. "It has been fine for a month" is not evidence. "It was right on all forty approvals and the log shows nothing blocked" is.
One report, built twice.
Tanvi's task had a catch, of the kind Imran liked best. She was to build the report twice.

The first version was a state machine. In this kind of workflow, her code fixed every step and every permitted move from one step to the next. It gathered the numbers, asked the model to draft, checked the draft against the numbers and sent it for approval. If the check failed, it tried once more, then stopped and said so.
The second version was a bounded agent. It was given a list of tools, a budget of steps and the task, and the model chose what to do.
They ran both on the same twenty past weeks, for which a person had already written the report.

Table 45.5: The state machine and the bounded agent on twenty weeks. Weeks with a correct report. State machine: 19 of 20. Bounded agent: 17 of 20. Median time. State machine: 40 seconds. Bounded agent: 75 seconds. Finding the cause of a failure. State machine: Minutes: the failing step is in the log. Bounded agent: Much longer: the whole trace must be read. An unusual week. State machine: Needs a code change. Bounded agent: Often adapts on its own.

For a fixed process such as a weekly report, Imran said, the machine with fixed steps wins. It is more accurate, faster, and it fails in a place that can be seen. The agent earns its keep when the steps really do vary from case to case. He asked where that would be here. Tanvi suggested looking into why one customer's count suddenly doubled. He agreed, and said to use the agent for that, in a corner, with a short budget.
Letting it out.
The last part of the task frightened her. A report that goes to customers needs a release gate, and Imran gave her the list.

The ordinary tests pass. The twenty weeks score at or above the line, with nothing new failing in the safety cases. Cost and time per run are within budget. The change goes first to one account in ten, behind a feature flag. That is a switch in the running system that turns a change on for some users and off for others, without a new release. A rollback trigger and the owner of an incident are written down.

A rollback trigger is a condition, written beforehand and measurable, that obliges someone to undo the release. Tanvi wrote hers: roll back if the share of reports that a customer marks as useful falls more than ten points below last week, or if any report goes to the wrong recipient. The person who decides was the engineer on call, who needed nobody's permission. The method was to switch the flag, and it would take under five minutes. They tested it once before launch, with a stopwatch.
They also wrote down how the system should respond to each kind of failure.

Table 45.6: Responses to failure. Retry. When: A temporary error. Example: A timeout; a rate limit. Degrade. When: One part is down but the rest works. Example: Send the report without the trend chart. Escalate. When: The output cannot be trusted. Example: The draft fails its check twice. Stop. When: An irreversible action looks wrong. Example: A report would go to five hundred people instead of five.

Imran stopped her pen at the last row. If the machine is about to do something it cannot take back, and the action looks wrong, it stops. A delayed report is an annoyance. A report sent to the wrong five hundred is a letter from a lawyer.

And if something did go wrong, someone would write an incident review within two days. It is a page saying what happened, why, and which check would have caught it. It names a check, not a person to blame.

Tanvi finished on a Friday. The first report went to a single account, behind the flag, at four in the afternoon, and Imran walked past her desk three times without saying anything. It arrived, and it was right. She switched the flag off, and then on again, to prove that she could.
Chapter summary.
An AI product needs about eleven jobs done for it. The useful way to think of tools is as slots to fill, choosing one tool per job by what it must do and what must never go wrong.

Two audits belong to every stack: check ten claims from any AI summary against their sources, and write down for every tool what it stores and where its keys live. The model is one part of a product. The rest, the harness, has seven parts: context, tools, state, orchestration, policy, evals and observability. Most quality problems live there. Coding assistants run a simple loop, use a few general tools, keep project rules in a file, ask permission for risky acts and rely above all on a verifier. Tool access should be an allowlist, narrow in scope, with approval for anything that cannot be undone, and widened only on evidence chosen beforehand. For a fixed process a state machine usually beats an agent, and the choice should be measured on the same cases. A change goes out behind a gate and a flag, with a rollback trigger, a named owner and a plan for each kind of failure.
With the tools in place, the team can put the product in front of real people.
